title: Input and maths
bridge: C reads input with `scanf("%d", &n);`: the same format codes as `printf`, and `&` before the variable (it gives scanf the variable's *address* so it can fill it in; pointers explain this later). Use `%lf` to read a double. `scanf` returns how many values it read.
lesson:
```
int seconds;
scanf("%d", &seconds);          /* the user types 125 */
printf("%d min %d s\n", seconds / 60, seconds % 60);

double kg;
scanf("%lf", &kg);              /* %lf to READ a double (printf uses %f) */
```

The `&` matters: `scanf("%d", seconds)` without it compiles (with a warning) and then crashes. scanf needs to know *where* to put the number, and `&seconds` is "where seconds lives".

`scanf` returns the number of values it managed to read, so you can tell when input runs out:

```
int x;
while (scanf("%d", &x) == 1) { ... }   /* read numbers until there are none */
```

**Rounding up** with ints: `(kg + bag_size - 1) / bag_size`. More maths is in `<math.h>`: `sqrt`, `pow`, `fabs`, `round`.

exercises.title: Minutes and seconds
exercises.prompt: Read a number of seconds and print it as minutes and seconds, e.g. 125 prints: 2 min 5 s

exercises.title: Bags needed
exercises.prompt: Write int bags_needed(int kg, int bag_size): how many bags to hold all of it (a part-full bag still counts).

tests.hint_if_fail: 100 / 30 is 3 and leaves 10 kg over. Round up.
